messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

reply.reasoning:
*   Goal: Power a load RL from a piezo harvester.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{V}$
        *   $\text{Ripple } V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$
        *   $\text{Startup } t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$
        *   $\text{Settled } dv \le 0.02\text{V}$
    *   Piezo: $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$, $C_p = 25\text{nF}$ (nominal), $R_{leak} = 20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Conditions: S1 (nominal), S2 (heavy load), S3 (strong excitation/light load), S4 (weak excitation), S5 (low freq), S6 (hot/higher $C_p$).
    *   Reference: Full-bridge rectifier (FBR) fails S2 (too low $V_{avg}$), S3 (too high $V_{max}$), S4 (too low $V_{avg}$), S5 (not settled).

    *   Open circuit voltage $V_{oc} = I_p / (2\pi f C_p)$.
    *   Nominal: $50\text{uA} / (2\pi \cdot 100\text{Hz} \cdot 25\text{nF}) \approx 3.18\text{V}$.
    *   S3 (Strong): $100\text{uA} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}) \approx 6.36\text{V}$.
    *   S4 (Weak): $30\text{uA} / (2\pi \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF}) \approx 1.91\text{V}$.
    *   Observation: With $V_{oc} \approx 1.9\text{V}$ in S4 and diode drops ($\sim 0.25\text{V} \cdot 2 = 0.5\text{V}$ for a bridge), reaching $1.8\text{V}$ at the output is extremely difficult with a simple passive bridge. We need something more efficient or a way to boost/regulate.

    *   *Passive Full Bridge (FBR):* Too many losses, no regulation.
    *   *Synchronous Switch Harvesting on Inductor (SSHI):* Uses an inductor and switches to flip the voltage on $C_p$, effectively increasing the harvested energy.
    *   *Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE):* Extracts charge at peaks.
    *   *Zener Clamp:* Necessary for S3 to prevent $V_{out}$ from exceeding $3.6\text{V}$.

    *   **Design 1: SSHI (Parallel SSHI or similar)**
        *   Basic SSHI: Inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with $C_p$ to invert voltage.
        *   Rectification: A diode/capacitor stage to store the flipped energy.
        *   Given the low $V_{oc}$ in S4, SSHI's ability to increase the effective voltage is key.
        *   Topology: Piezo $\to$ Rectifier $\to$ $C_{out}$. Parallel to piezo: Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ (SYNC).
        *   Correction: A standard SSHI uses a switch and inductor to invert $C_p$ voltage at the peaks.
        *   Let's try a simplified SSHI:
            1.  Piezo $pzp, pzn$.
            2.  Inductor $L$ between $pzp$ and $n1$.
            3.  Switch $S$ between $n1$ and $pzn$.
            4.  SYNC $G$ triggers $S$ at peaks.
            5.  Half-wave or Full-wave rectifier to $C_{out}$. Since $V_{oc}$ is low, every bit counts. Let's use a full bridge but with low-drop DSCH.
            6.  Zener $DZ33$ on $V_{out}$ to clamp S3.

    *   **Design 2: SECE-like or Simple Boosted SSHI**
        *   Alternative to full bridge: a more efficient rectifier or a different SSHI configuration.
        *   Let's try a "Parallel-SSHI" where the inductor is used to flip the piezo voltage before rectification.
        *   Actually, the most robust for low-voltage piezo is often a synchronous rectifier or a very efficient charge pump, but we only have SYNC switches and diodes.

    *   **Design 3: Optimized Bridge with Zener and larger $C_{out}$**
        *   FBR failed S2 and S4. S2 is heavy load, S4 is weak excitation.
        *   Wait, SSHI helps with $V_{oc}$. Let's refine the SSHI topology.
        *   SSHI topology:
            - Piezo nodes: $pzp, pzn$.
            - Rectifier: $D_1(pzp, out), D_2(pzn, out), D_3(0, pzp), D_4(0, pzn)$.
            - SSHI flip: Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo.
            - $L$ from $pzp$ to $mid$, $S$ from $mid$ to $pzn$.
            - SYNC $G$: `edges: both`, `ton` tuned to $\pi\sqrt{L C_p}$.
            - Storage: $C_{out}$ from $out$ to $0$.
            - Clamp: $D_{zener}$ from $0$ to $out$ (DZ33).

    *   S2 (Heavy load): $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$. SSHI increases available power.
    *   S3 (Strong): $V_{max} \le 3.6\text{V}$. DZ33 clamp handles this.
    *   S4 (Weak): $V_{avg} \ge 1.8\text{V}$. This is the hardest. SSHI boosts the effective $V_{oc}$.
    *   S5 (Low freq): Settled $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$. $C_{out}$ needs to be large enough to filter ripple.
    *   S6 (Hot): Nominal performance.

    *   $L \approx 10\text{mH}$ (within $0.01\text{H}$ limit).
    *   $C_{out} \approx 4.7\mu\text{F}$ (within $4.7\text{e-05}\text{F}$ limit).
    *   $T_{on} \approx \pi\sqrt{L C_p} \approx \pi\sqrt{10\text{mH} \cdot 25\text{nF}} \approx \pi\sqrt{2.5\cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 1.5\cdot 10^{-5}\text{s}$.

    *   Design 1: Parallel SSHI with Full Bridge and Zener Clamp.
    *   Design 2: Parallel SSHI with Half-Wave Rectifier (might be too inefficient for S4, but lets try a slightly different SSHI if I can). Actually, let's stick to Full Bridge for maximum extraction.
    *   Design 3: A different SSHI variant? Maybe "Series SSHI"? No, Parallel is simpler. How about a charge-extraction circuit (SECE)?
        - SECE: Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ to transfer charge from $C_p$ to $C_{out}$.
        - $L$ from $pzp$ to $mid$, $S$ from $mid$ to $out$, $S2$ from $pzn$ to $mid2$, $S3$ from $mid2$ to $out$. This is getting complex.
    *   Let's focus on a high-quality SSHI.

    *   Wait, the prompt allows 16 components.
    *   Full Bridge (4x DSCH) + Zener (1x DZ33) + SSHI (1x L, 1x S, 1x SYNC) + Filter (1x C). Total: 8 components. This is well within limits.

    *   For a full bridge:
        $D1: pzp \to out$
        $D2: pzn \to out$
        $D3: 0 \to pzp$
        $D4: 0 \to pzn$
        Wait, the prompt says: `full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]`. Let's follow that exactly.
        $D1: pzp, out$
        $D2: pzn, out$
        $D3: 0, pzp$
        $D4: 0, pzn$
        Wait, let's check the polarity.
        Current from piezo $pzp \to pzn$.
        Positive half: $pzp$ is $+$, $pzn$ is $-$. Current flows $pzp \to D1 \to out \to C_{out} \to 0 \to D4 \to pzn$. (Correct)
        Negative half: $pzp$ is $-$, $pzn$ is $+$. Current flows $pzn \to D2 \to out \to C_{out} \to 0 \to D3 \to pzp$. (Correct)

    *   Wait, if $V_{oc}$ is very low (S4 $\approx 1.9\text{V}$), the diode drops ($0.25 \cdot 2 = 0.5\text{V}$) leave only $1.4\text{V}$, which is below $1.8\text{V}$.
    *   SSHI helps by flipping $V_{Cp}$. If $V_{Cp}$ reaches $V_{peak}$, and we flip it to $-V_{peak}$, the voltage swing is $2V_{peak}$. This increases the voltage the rectifier "sees".
    *   In SSHI, the inductor $L$ is switched in parallel with $C_p$ at the peaks to invert the voltage.
    *   Circuit:
        $L$ from $pzp$ to $n1$.
        $S$ from $n1$ to $pzn$.
        $S$ is closed at the peaks.
        This flips the voltage on $C_p$.
        The rectifier then captures the resulting voltage.

    *   Let's double-check the SYNC: `ton` is $1\text{e-7}$ to $0.001$. `phase` is $-0.25$ to $0.25$. `edges` is `both`.

    *   Another option for S4: a Synchronous Rectifier? But we only have 2 SYNCs. We can use them for SSHI or for rectification. SSHI is generally more powerful for piezo.

    *   S3 $V_{max}$ can reach $6.36\text{V}$. $V_{out}$ must be $\le 3.6\text{V}$. DZ33 zener from $0$ to $out$ (cathode on $out$) will clamp it at $3.3\text{V}$.

    *   S2/S4 $V_{avg}$: $C_{out}$ needs to be large to maintain $1.8\text{V}$ with low current. $C_{out} = 10\mu\text{F}$ (Wait, limit is $4.7\mu\text{F}$). Let's use $4.7\mu\text{F}$.

    *   What if the Full Bridge is still too lossy?
        A half-bridge (1 diode) would have lower drop (0.25V vs 0.5V) but only harvest half the cycles. For $V_{oc} = 1.9\text{V}$, $1.9 - 0.25 = 1.65\text{V}$, still below $1.8\text{V}$.
        So the only way to get above $1.8\text{V}$ in S4 is to increase the voltage using the SSHI flip.

    *   Let's refine the SSHI flip circuit:
        Piezo: $pzp, pzn$
        L1: $pzp, n1$
        S1: $n1, pzn$
        Ctrl: G1 (SYNC)
        This will invert the voltage across $pzp$ and $pzn$.

    *   Wait, there's a subtle point in SSHI: the inductor flip usually happens *before* the rectifier.
        If we have a full bridge, the piezo is connected to the bridge. The inductor-switch combo is in parallel with the piezo. This is "Parallel SSHI". It works.

    *   Let's try three variations:
        1.  Parallel SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener + $C_{out}$.
        2.  Parallel SSHI + Half-bridge (single diode $pzp \to out$) + Zener + $C_{out}$. (Less energy, but lower drop).
        3.  A different inductor placement for SSHI (e.g., Series SSHI). Series SSHI often performs better.
            In Series SSHI:
            Inductor $L$ is in series with the piezo.
            Switch $S$ is in parallel with the piezo.
            No, let's stick to Parallel SSHI for now as it's more standard. Let's just vary the rectifier for Proposal 2.

    *   Wait, is there any other way to boost voltage? A charge pump? With only 2 SYNCs and diodes, it's hard. SSHI is the best bet.

    *   Let's re-verify S4 again. $V_{oc} = 1.91\text{V}$.
        With SSHI, the voltage across the piezo can be increased.
        The voltage at the peaks is $V_{peak}$. After flipping, it becomes $-V_{peak}$. The total swing is $2 V_{peak}$.
        The rectifier sees this and can potentially charge $C_{out}$ to a higher voltage than $V_{oc}$.

    *   Let's check the components for Proposal 1 (Parallel SSHI):
        D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
        D2: pzn, out (DSCH)
        D3: 0, pzp (DSCH)
        D4: 0, pzn (DSCH)
        DZ1: 0, out (DZ33)
        L1: pzp, n1
        S1: n1, pzn
        G1: SYNC (ton=3e-5, phase=0, edges=both)
        C1: out, 0 (value=4.7uF)

    *   Let's check the components for Proposal 2 (Half-Bridge SSHI):
        D1: pzp, out (DSCH)
        DZ1: 0, out (DZ33)
        L1: pzp, n1
        S1: n1, pzn
        G1: SYNC (ton=3e-5, phase=0, edges=both)
        C1: out, 0 (value=4.7uF)
        (Wait, this will only harvest half the energy. S2/S4 might fail).

    *   Let's try Proposal 3 (SSHI with a different SYNC phase):
        Same as Proposal 1, but maybe `phase=0.1` or something? No, the evolution strategy will optimize `ton` and `phase`. I just need to provide the connectivity.

    *   Wait, what if I use two inductors? No, I only have 2 SYNCs.

    *   Let's reconsider the Full Bridge. If $V_{oc} = 1.9\text{V}$, the voltage at the output of a full bridge (without SSHI) is $V_{out} \approx V_{oc} - 0.5\text{V} = 1.4\text{V}$.
        With SSHI, the voltage across the piezo can be boosted.
        In Parallel SSHI, the voltage is flipped. The rectifier then charges the capacitor. The maximum voltage $V_{out}$ can reach is roughly the peak voltage of the piezo *after* flipping, minus diode drops.
        $V_{peak\_sshi} \approx V_{oc} \cdot (\text{something } > 1)$.

    *   Wait, if $V_{oc} = 1.9\text{V}$, then $V_{peak} = 1.9\text{V}$. If we flip it perfectly, the voltage goes from $1.9\text{V}$ to $-1.9\text{V}$. The rectifier's input is $1.9\text{V}$. It still only sees $1.9\text{V}$!
        Wait, SSHI doesn't increase the *peak* voltage; it increases the *amount of charge* extracted per cycle by preventing the piezo from discharging back through the diodes.
        Actually, for low $V_{oc}$, the most important thing is to minimize the diode drop.
        What if we use a SYNC switch instead of a diode for rectification?
        Synchronous Rectification:
        S1: pzp, out
        S2: pzn, out
        But then we can't use SYNC for SSHI. We only have 2 SYNCs.
        If we use S1 and S2 for rectification, we can't have an inductor flip.

        Let's think... if $V_{oc} = 1.9\text{V}$ and we need $V_{out} = 1.8\text{V}$, we only have $0.1\text{V}$ of headroom.
        A full bridge (DSCH) drops $\sim 0.5\text{V}$.
        A half bridge (DSCH) drops $\sim 0.25\text{V}$.
        If we use a half bridge, $V_{out} \approx 1.9 - 0.25 = 1.65\text{V}$. Still too low.
        The only way to get $V_{out} = 1.8\text{V}$ when $V_{oc} = 1.9\text{V}$ is to have almost zero drop.
        This means synchronous rectification.
        But if we use synchronous rectification, we lose the SSHI boost.
        Is the SSHI boost enough to overcome the $0.5\text{V}$ drop?
        In Parallel SSHI, the voltage across the piezo *does* increase because the inductor flip prevents the voltage from returning to zero.
        The voltage $V_{Cp}$ can reach $V_{out} + V_{diode}$ at the peak.
        Actually, the standard SSHI formula shows $V_{out}$ can be significantly higher than $V_{oc}$ if the flipping is efficient.

    *   Let's try these three topologies:
        1. Parallel SSHI + Full Bridge + Zener Clamp + $C_{out}$
        2. Parallel SSHI + Half-Bridge + Zener Clamp + $C_{out}$
        3. SECE-like (Synchronous Charge Extraction):
           S1: pzp, out (closed at peak)
           S2: pzn, out (closed at peak)
           Inductor $L$: pzp, pzn (No, this is just a short)
           SECE is usually:
           $L$ from $pzp$ to $n1$, $S1$ from $n1$ to $out$.
           $L2$ from $pzn$ to $n2$, $S2$ from $n2$ to $out$.
           But we only have 2 SYNCs and can't have 2 inductors easily without more switches.

    *   Let's stick to Parallel SSHI + Full Bridge for the first one. It's the most likely to provide enough power for S2.
    *   For the second one, let's try Parallel SSHI + Half-Bridge.
    *   For the third one, let's try a different SSHI configuration: "Series SSHI".
        In Series SSHI:
        $L$ is in series with the piezo.
        The rectifier is then connected.
        Actually, the most common SSHI is the one I described (Parallel).
        Let's try a variant: "SSHI with a capacitor-based charge pump" (not possible with SYNC).
        How about just Parallel SSHI with a very large $C_{out}$? (already planned).

    *   Wait! I have another idea for Proposal 3.
        What if I use the SYNC switches as a synchronous rectifier?
        S1: pzp, out
        S2: pzn, out
        G1: edges: pos, phase: 0
        G2: edges: neg, phase: 0
        Then $V_{out}$ will be almost exactly $V_{oc}$.
        For S4, $V_{oc} = 1.9\text{V}$, so $V_{out} = 1.9\text{V}$. (Success!)
        For S3, $V_{oc} = 6.3\text{V}$, so $V_{out} = 6.3\text{V}$. (Need Zener!)
        For S2 (heavy load), we have no inductor boost, but we have zero diode drop.
        Let's check S2: $P_{load} = V^2/RL = 1.8^2 / 150\text{k} = 21.6\mu\text{W}$.
        Can the piezo provide $21.6\mu\text{W}$ without SSHI?
        $P_{avg} \approx 2 \cdot f \cdot C_p \cdot V_{oc}^2 = 2 \cdot 100 \cdot 25\text{nF} \cdot 3.2^2 \approx 51\mu\text{W}$.
        Yes, it can! Synchronous rectification might actually be more effective than SSHI for these specific low-voltage conditions.

    *   Let's refine the Synchronous Rectifier (Proposal 3):
        S1: pzp, out
        S2: pzn, out
        G1: SYNC, edges: pos, phase: 0, ton: 0.005 (max)
        G2: SYNC, edges: neg, phase: 0, ton: 0.005 (max)
        C1: out, 0
        DZ1: 0, out (Zener)
        This replaces the 4 diodes with 2 switches.

    *   Wait, the SYNC `ton` is limited to $0.001\text{s}$.
        $0.001\text{s}$ at $100\text{Hz}$ (period $0.01\text{s}$) is $10\%$ of the period.
        That's not enough for a full half-cycle rectification!
        So synchronous rectification using SYNC won't work.
        The switches only close for a tiny burst.
        This means the "synchronous rectifier" would actually just be a "synchronous charge extractor".

    *   Okay, so back to SSHI. The `ton` is specifically designed for $L-C$ resonance ($\pi\sqrt{L C_p}$).
        So Parallel SSHI is the way to go.

    *   Let's re-verify the Parallel SSHI:
        - Piezo $C_p$ is in parallel with the rectifier.
        - Inductor $L$ and Switch $S$ are in parallel with $C_p$.
        - When $S$ closes, $C_p$ and $L$ form a resonant circuit, flipping the voltage on $C_p$.
        - The rectifier then captures the energy.
        - This increases the average voltage $V_{out}$ and the power.
